title: Why the river runs brown in November
teaches: What a river carries, the speed a grain needs to move (Hjulström), and the Elwha's century of trapped sediment
summary: **A river carries three loads.** Minerals dissolved in the water, clay, silt and fine sand held up by eddies (the suspended load that turns it brown), and sand and gravel rolling along the bed.

**Bigger grains need faster water, except the smallest.** From fine sand up to boulders each step up in size needs a faster current, but clay flakes stick together and hide in the slow water at the bed, so clay needs a faster current than fine sand: the dip in Hjulström's 1935 chart.
**Once moving, fine grains stay up.** Clay sinks about a centimetre an hour, so it rides on to a lake or the sea while gravel and sand drop out as soon as the current slackens.
**November storms bring both speed and supply.** Faster, deeper water lifts more and bigger grains, and rain, eroding banks and landslides deliver fresh soil to the channel.
**A few flood days move most of the year's sediment.** At a gram of mud a litre, a river in flood carries tonnes every second.
**Glaciers grind rock to flour.** It is fine enough to stay suspended, which is why glacier-fed rivers run milky in summer and Diablo Lake is turquoise.
**A reservoir is a sediment trap.** Behind the Elwha's dams of 1913 and 1927 the slowed river dropped its sand and gravel for a century, starving the channel and the coast below.
**A delta is supply against waves.** With the dams removed from 2011 to 2014, the stored sediment came down, and the Elwha's delta grew back within a few years.

blocks.text: In September 2011 crews began taking apart two concrete dams on the Elwha River, on the north side of the Olympic Peninsula. Through 2012 the river below them ran the colour of milky coffee, and a brown plume spread from its mouth into the Strait of Juan de Fuca, a cloud of muddy water drifting out over the blue-grey sea, plain to see from the hills above Port Angeles and from satellites. Within a few years a new beach and a broad fan of sand and gravel had built out at the river mouth, where for decades there had been only a narrow, eroding strip of cobbles.

The mud, sand and gravel came out of the two lakes behind the dams, where the river had been dropping them for nearly a century. To see why it dropped them there, and why the same river that runs clear in August runs brown in November, start with what a river carries and what it takes to move a grain.

A river moves three kinds of load. The first is invisible: minerals dissolved from rock and soil, the **dissolved load**. Rivers draining the hard rocks of the Cascades and Olympics carry little of it, which is why Seattle's tap water is unusually soft, low in the dissolved calcium and magnesium that leave scale in a kettle. The second is the [[suspended load|sediment]]: clay, silt and fine sand held up in the water by its eddies. That is what makes a river brown. The third is the [[bed load|sediment]]: coarser sand, gravel and stones too heavy to stay up, which roll, slide and bounce along the bottom. Fine sand sits on the line between the two: it rides in the water in a fast current and hops along the bed in a slow one. Stand beside a gravel river in flood and you can sometimes hear it, a knocking of stones under the water.

blocks.caption: A river in cross-section, carrying its three loads. The suspended grains are most crowded near the bed, where the current lifts them; the bed load moves only along the bottom.

blocks.text: Geologists sort grains by size. **Clay** is finer than about 4 thousandths of a millimetre, a flake too small to see. **Silt** runs up to about a sixteenth of a millimetre, gritty between the teeth but too small to make out one by one. **Sand** runs from there to 2 millimetres, and anything bigger is **gravel**: pebbles, then cobbles, then boulders.

**How much mud?** A brown river in flood easily carries a gram of sediment in every litre, and some carry several. Take a large river in flood running 3,000 cubic metres a second, lesson 2's discharge, about 100,000 cubic feet a second, a big flood on the Skagit. A cubic metre is a thousand litres, so at a gram a litre that is 3 tonnes of sediment every second, more than 10,000 tonnes an hour: a large dump truck, which holds 15 to 20 tonnes, every five or six seconds. On rivers like this a handful of flood days each winter carries most of the year's sediment.[^gauge]

Faster water carries more, and the reason is easy to see. A grain resting on the bed stays put until the push of the current and the lift of its eddies beat the grain's weight and the grip of its neighbours. Bigger grains are heavier, so they need faster water. The question is what happens at the small end.

In 1935 a young Swedish geographer, Filip Hjulström, finished a doctoral thesis at Uppsala on the River Fyris, a small river that runs through the town. To understand what the Fyris moved and where it dropped it, he gathered every measurement he could find of the current needed to move grains of each size, and drew them all on one chart: grain size along the bottom, on a scale where each step is ten times the last,[^log] and current speed up the side. One line marked the speed that starts a grain moving off the bed. A second, lower line marked the speed below which a moving grain settles out. The figure redraws his chart, with a grain on a river bed underneath. It starts with fine sand in a current of 30 centimetres a second, the dot on the chart; the current slider runs from half a centimetre to 5 metres a second. The lines stay hidden until you guess: does a current that moves fine sand also lift a bed of clay?

blocks.caption: Hjulström's chart, redrawn as a model for water about a metre deep. The solid line is the current that starts a grain moving; below the dashed line a moving grain settles out. Choose a grain and set the current; the grain on the bed below does what the chart says.
blocks.task: Guess, then find a current, in metres a second, that lifts clay

blocks.text: Down to fine sand, the line does what you would expect: smaller grains need less speed, until grains about a quarter of a millimetre across move in a current of 20 centimetres a second or so. Then the line turns up. Silt needs a faster current than fine sand, and a bed of clay needs much faster, a metre or two a second, though each flake is a hundred times smaller than a sand grain. For clay the line is really a broad band: a soft new layer of mud lifts more easily, a packed old one far less.[^curve]

Two things hold the smallest grains down. Clay particles are thin flakes that cling to one another by weak electrical forces, so a bed of clay behaves less like loose grains and more like a sticky sheet that the current has to tear. And very small grains lie inside the thin layer of slow water right against the bed, where the current barely reaches them, the way dust stays on a car's paint at motorway speed, because the air right against the paint is almost still. Lift them by some other means, a boot, a wave, a slumping bank, and they stay up a long time, because they sink so slowly.

That is the chart's other lesson. At the small end the two lines are far apart. Once moving, a clay flake stays in the water until the current is almost still: in calm water it sinks about a centimetre an hour, and the slightest eddy keeps it up.[^stokes] Fine sand settles within a minute when the current slows, gravel at once. So a river sorts what it carries. Gravel drops first, on bars at the inside of bends and where the valley flattens; sand further on; and the silt and clay ride on to a lake or the sea. In salt water the clay flakes clump together and sink much faster, so most of it settles on the sea floor within some kilometres of the river mouth.

**In a jar.** Put a handful of mud from a creek bank or a garden bed into a tall jar of water, shake it hard and set it down. Any gravel hits the bottom at once and sand within a few seconds. Silt takes minutes to hours, and the water above stays cloudy with clay overnight or longer. The layers that form, coarse at the bottom and fine on top, are the river's sorting done in one jar.

A river in August is mostly baseflow (lesson 3), low and slow, and clear. Its current is too slow to lift anything but the finest silt, and there is little to lift, because nothing new has reached the channel for weeks. The first big storms of autumn change both. The river rises from its August trickle, and lesson 2's discharge goes up tenfold or a hundredfold; deeper water also runs faster, so the current climbs Hjulström's chart into sand and then gravel. At the same time rain washes soil off bare ground and road cuts, floods undercut the banks, and in steep valleys saturated slopes slide, tipping fresh mud straight into the channel. November's brown is soil the storm has just delivered, carried by a current fast enough to keep it up.

Glacier-fed rivers have a second colour. Under a moving glacier, stones frozen into the ice grind the bedrock to a powder of silt and clay called **glacial flour**. Meltwater carries it out mainly in summer, when the glaciers melt fastest, so rivers draining Mount Rainier, Mount Baker and the North Cascades run milky grey through July and August, even in dry weather. The flour is so fine that it barely settles even in still water. In Diablo Lake on the Skagit, the grains still hanging in the water scatter sunlight and turn the lake an opaque turquoise.

Volcanoes add their own supply. The rivers off Mount Rainier, the Puyallup, Carbon and White, carry so much sand and gravel from the mountain's loose slopes and old mudflows that their beds have been building upward for decades, raising the flood risk in the valleys below. The Geology course follows the mudflows themselves.

The Elwha runs about 70 kilometres (45 miles) from the snowfields of the Olympic Mountains to the Strait, steep and fast for most of the way, through young mountains that shed sediment quickly. In 1913 a dam was finished across its lower canyon, about 8 kilometres from the mouth, to make electricity for Port Angeles and its mills. A second, taller dam, Glines Canyon, followed in 1927, about 21 kilometres up. Behind them lay two reservoirs, Lake Aldwell and Lake Mills.

A reservoir is a river slowed almost to stillness, and Hjulström's chart says what happens next. Where the Elwha's current died at the head of each lake, its gravel and sand dropped at once and built a delta out into the lake, and the finer silt settled over the lake floor beyond it. Only some of the finest mud got through. For close to a century the dams held back nearly all the river's sand and gravel. By the 2000s about 20 million cubic metres of sediment had piled up in the two lakes, enough to cover a football pitch nearly three kilometres deep. A cubic metre of it weighs about a tonne and a half, so that is something like 30 million tonnes.

Below the dams the river was starved. With no new gravel coming down, floods kept carrying away what was in the channel and left it scoured to large cobbles. At the coast the waves kept taking sand away along the shore, and the river no longer replaced it. The beach at the mouth wore back to cobbles, and the long spit that shelters Port Angeles harbour, Ediz Hook, began to waste away (lesson 14). The dams also blocked salmon from all but the lowest 8 kilometres (5 miles) of the river, a story for the next course.

After decades of pressure, much of it from the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, Congress passed a law in 1992 to restore the river, and in September 2011 both dams began to come down. Crews took them down in stages, cutting and blasting away a few metres of concrete at a time and then pausing, so the river could carry off the stored sediment gradually rather than all at once.[^condit] The Elwha Dam was gone by the spring of 2012. The last piece of Glines Canyon, at 64 metres (210 feet) the tallest dam ever removed until then, was blasted out in August 2014.

blocks.task: Press Play, or drag the step slider, through all four stages

stages.label: Before 1913
stages.text: The river carries sand and gravel down to its mouth, and waves move some of it east along the shore toward Ediz Hook.

stages.label: 1913 to 2011
stages.text: Two dams and their lakes trap the river's sand and gravel. The channel below them scours to cobbles, and the delta and the beach east of it wear back.
With the dams coming down, the river cuts into the old lake beds. The mud goes out to sea in a brown plume; the sand and gravel follow more slowly along the bed.
A new delta and sand beach have built out at the mouth, and some of the sand is drifting east toward Ediz Hook.

blocks.text: With the dams going, the river went to work on the old lake beds, and Hjulström's chart says what to expect. The fine silt and clay that had settled in still water were lifted at once by a flowing river and carried to the sea in suspension: the plume of 2012. The sand and gravel took years to work down, rolling and hopping along the bed in short bursts during floods, filling pools and burying the scoured cobble bed. In the first two years the river moved roughly a third of the stored sediment, around 10 million tonnes, out of the old reservoirs, one of the largest releases of sediment from a dam removal ever measured.

At the mouth, a delta is a race between supply and removal. The river brings sediment; the waves and currents carry it away along the coast. While the dams stood, removal won, and the delta shrank. The figure runs that race as a model, from 1900 to 2030. Before you play it, guess how long the delta takes to grow back once the dams are out.

blocks.caption: The Elwha's mouth seen from above, a model: each year the river adds what reaches the coast and the waves take away a share of the delta. Play from 1900 to 2030, or keep the dams in to compare.
blocks.task: Guess, then play on past 2016 with the dams out

blocks.text: The real delta grew by tens of hectares in the first few years after removal, pushing the shore seaward by hundreds of metres in places, and the beaches east of the mouth turned from cobbles back toward sand and gravel. Some of that sand is drifting east toward Ediz Hook. As the old lake beds settled and the pulse of stored sediment passed, the delta's growth slowed, and the river is settling back toward its natural supply. Its plume now comes in November, with the storms, like any other river's.

blocks.caption: Six questions on what rivers carry
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Which part of a river's load makes it look brown?
choices: Suspended load: fine grains held up by the eddies
Dissolved load: minerals from the rocks and soil
Bed load: sand and gravel stirred off the bottom
items.why: Dissolved minerals are invisible, and the bed load stays on the bottom. The fine grains spread through the water are what you see.

items.ask: On Hjulström's chart, why does a bed of clay need a faster current to start moving than a bed of fine sand?
choices: Clay flakes cling together and lie in slow water against the bed
Clay grains are denser than sand grains and need a harder push
Clay sinks faster once lifted, so it drops back before it travels
items.why: Cohesion and the slow layer at the bed hold clay down. Once it is lifted, clay sinks far more slowly than sand, not faster.

items.ask: A flood current of 1 metre a second carrying gravel, sand, silt and clay enters a lake and slows to 1 centimetre a second. By Hjulström's chart, what settles out?
choices: The gravel and sand; the silt and clay stay in the water
The gravel only; the sand, silt and clay stay up
All of it, since 1 cm/s is too slow to carry anything
items.why: Below the dashed line a moving grain settles. At 1 cm/s that takes in gravel and sand, but silt and clay, once moving, stay up in a current far slower still, so a river sorts its load.

items.ask: Why do rivers draining Mount Rainier run milky grey in midsummer, even in dry weather?
choices: Rock ground to flour under glaciers, carried by meltwater, too fine to settle
Ash and soil washed off the volcano's bare upper slopes by melting snow
Minerals dissolved out of the volcanic rock by the warm summer meltwater
items.why: Glacial flour is silt and clay so fine it stays suspended. It comes out with the meltwater, which peaks in summer.

items.ask: Why did the beach at the Elwha's mouth wear back while the dams stood?
choices: Waves kept carrying sand along the shore, and the river stopped replacing it
Clear water released below the dams ran faster and cut into the delta
The reservoirs held back the winter floods that had built the beach up
items.why: A delta holds its size while supply matches what the waves remove. The reservoirs trapped the supply, so removal won.

items.ask: After the Elwha dams came out, mud reached the sea in the first months, while gravel took years to work down the channel. Why?
choices: Lifted mud rides with the water; gravel moves only in floods, in short hops
The gravel lay under the mud in the old lakes and was uncovered last
The river had to fill its scoured pools with mud before gravel could pass
items.why: Suspended load travels with the water. Bed load moves only while the current is above its starting speed, in floods, and then in short hops along the bed.

gauge.title: Measuring the mud
gauge.text: The USGS measures suspended sediment by dipping bottles at set depths across a river and weighing what settles out, and in between by sensors that record how cloudy the water is (its turbidity) every few minutes. On the Elwha such a sensor at McDonald Bridge, below the old Elwha Dam, recorded the dam removal from start to finish.

log.title: Each step ten times the last
log.text: Grains in a river run from clay flakes about a thousandth of a millimetre across to boulders a metre or more across, a millionfold range. On an ordinary scale everything but the boulders would be squashed against the left edge, so the chart gives each tenfold step the same room: 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100 millimetres are evenly spaced, and the chart stops at 100 mm cobbles. The current runs up the side the same way.

curve.title: What the chart assumes
curve.text: Hjulström's lines are for loose grains of one size, in water about a metre deep, with the current as the average over the depth. Real beds mix sizes, and a packed clay bed can need far more speed than a soft one, so his upper line for clay is really a broad band, as the lesson says. Åke Sundborg redrew the chart in 1956 with more data; later engineers replaced it with a measure of the force on the bed, but the shape, with its dip near fine sand, survived.

stokes.title: How fast grains sink
stokes.text: George Stokes worked out in 1851 how fast a small sphere falls through a liquid: the speed goes with the square of its diameter. A typical clay flake, 2 thousandths of a millimetre across, sinks about a centimetre an hour, a silt grain ten times wider about a metre an hour, and a fine sand grain a couple of centimetres a second. In sea water, clay flakes stick together into clumps that sink much faster, which is why most of a river's clay settles within some kilometres of its mouth and a plume fades as it spreads.

condit.title: The other way to take out a dam
condit.text: A month after work began on the Elwha, Condit Dam on the White Salmon River, a Columbia tributary, was removed the opposite way: on 26 October 2011 engineers blasted a hole in its base and drained the reservoir in a couple of hours, sending much of its sediment downstream in one rush. Geologists have since compared the slow removal and the sudden one closely, to learn how quickly a river carries away sediment stored behind a dam.
